desc: Napoleone di Buonaparte is born into minor Corsican nobility, a year after Genoa handed the island to France. At nine he is sent to military school on the mainland, speaking French with an accent he never fully loses.
fact: He wasn't short. At about 1.69 m he was average for his time. The “five foot two” legend comes from mixing up French and English inches, helped along by British cartoonists.

cmd: France: Jacques Dugommier, with Captain Bonaparte commanding the artillery
Coalition: Samuel Hood (Britain) and Federico Gravina (Spain)
desc: A young artillery officer spots the key to the royalist-held port: take the heights, put guns on them, and the British fleet has to leave. It works, and at 24 he is promoted to brigadier general.
fact: He took a bayonet wound to the thigh in the final assault, one of the very few wounds of his whole career.

cmd: Convention: Paul Barras, with Bonaparte commanding the guns
desc: Royalist crowds march on the National Convention. Bonaparte, put in charge of its defence, turns cannon on the streets around the church of Saint-Roch. The revolt collapses, and within months he is married to Joséphine and commanding the Army of Italy.
fact: The famous line “a whiff of grapeshot” wasn't his. The historian Thomas Carlyle coined it decades later.

cmd: France: Bonaparte, with Masséna and Laharpe
desc: His first battle as commander-in-chief. Days after taking over the ragged Army of Italy he drives a wedge between the Austrian and Piedmontese forces in the Ligurian hills, and keeps them apart for the rest of the campaign.
fact: He is said to have remarked later that his own nobility dated from Montenotte: his career, not his birth, was his title.

desc: In his first campaign as a commander, his troops storm a bridge over the Adda river under Austrian fire. A small battle with a very large legend.
fact: His soldiers are said to have started calling him “le petit caporal” (the little corporal) after Lodi, and he later said it was here he first believed he was meant for great things.

cmd: France: Bonaparte, with Masséna and Augereau
desc: Three days of fighting in the marshes east of Verona finally push the Austrians back.
fact: Antoine-Jean Gros painted him leading the charge across the bridge with a flag. In reality the charge stalled, and he ended up being pulled out of a muddy ditch.

cmd: France: Bonaparte, with Masséna and Joubert
desc: A decisive win in the hills above Lake Garda ends Austria's last attempt to rescue besieged Mantua. By October Austria signs the Treaty of Campo Formio.
fact: Paris's Rue de Rivoli, one of the grandest streets in the city, is named after this battle.

cmd: Mamluk beys: Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey
desc: Hoping to threaten Britain's route to India, he invades Egypt and defeats the Mamluk cavalry within sight of the pyramids of Giza.
fact: He brought about 160 scholars on the expedition. French soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, and it passed to the British when the French in Egypt surrendered, which is why it's in the British Museum today.

desc: Admiral Nelson destroys the French fleet at anchor, leaving Bonaparte's army stranded in Egypt.
fact: The French flagship L'Orient blew up during the night battle. The blast was so huge that both sides reportedly stopped firing for a while afterwards.

cmd: Ottoman Empire: Jezzar Pasha, supported by Commodore Sidney Smith (Britain)
desc: Marching north into Ottoman Syria, he besieges the coastal fortress of Acre for two months and fails, with plague spreading through his army.
fact: The defence was helped by a British naval officer, Sidney Smith, and by a French royalist engineer who had been Bonaparte's classmate at military school.

cmd: Plotters: Bonaparte, Emmanuel Sieyès and Roger Ducos
The Directory and the councils of the Republic
desc: Back in France after slipping away from Egypt, he joins a coup against the Directory and comes out of it as First Consul, the most powerful man in France at 30.
fact: The coup nearly failed when deputies jostled and shouted him down. His brother Lucien saved it by calling in soldiers to clear the hall.

desc: After leading his army over the Alps, he is close to losing to the Austrians until General Desaix arrives with fresh troops in the afternoon. Desaix is killed; the battle is won.
fact: Jacques-Louis David painted him crossing the Great St Bernard Pass on a rearing stallion. He actually made the crossing on a sure-footed mule.

src: Musée du Louvre (David, Le Sacre de Napoléon)
desc: Napoleon is crowned Emperor of the French in Notre-Dame, with Pope Pius VII there to bless the ceremony.
fact: He placed the crown on his own head, then crowned Joséphine. David's enormous painting of the day shows his mother watching, though she didn't actually attend.

cmd: France and Spain: Vice-Admiral Pierre-Charles de Villeneuve and Admiral Federico Gravina
desc: Nelson's fleet crushes the combined French and Spanish navies, ending any real hope of invading Britain.
fact: Nelson was shot by a French marksman during the battle. His body was carried home preserved in a cask of brandy.

desc: The Grande Armée marches from the Channel coast to the Danube in a few weeks and encircles an Austrian army, which surrenders almost without a battle.
fact: His soldiers joked that the Emperor had found a new way to make war: with their legs instead of their bayonets.

cmd: Russia and Austria: Mikhail Kutuzov, with Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II present
desc: His masterpiece. He tempts the Russian and Austrian armies to attack his deliberately weakened right flank, then smashes their centre on the Pratzen Heights.
fact: It's called the Battle of the Three Emperors and was fought exactly a year after his coronation. Tolstoy set one of the most famous scenes in War and Peace on this battlefield.

cmd: France: Napoleon at Jena, Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout at Auerstedt
Prussia: Prince Hohenlohe at Jena, the Duke of Brunswick at Auerstedt (mortally wounded)
desc: Prussia is shattered in a single day. Napoleon beats one army at Jena while nearby, Marshal Davout defeats the main Prussian force at Auerstedt with far fewer men.
fact: The philosopher Hegel, finishing a book in Jena, watched Napoleon ride through town and described him as the world-soul on horseback.

cmd: Russia and Prussia: Levin August von Bennigsen
dispute: Both sides claimed it. The French held the field, the Russian army withdrew intact.
desc: A brutal fight against the Russians in a snowstorm. Both armies lose heavily and neither breaks.
fact: Marshal Murat led one of the biggest cavalry charges in history here, with around 10,000 horsemen.

desc: A decisive victory over the Russian army brings peace. Napoleon is now master of continental Europe.
fact: He and Tsar Alexander I met to make peace on a raft moored in the middle of the Neman river at Tilsit.

cmd: France: General Pierre Dupont de l'Étang
desc: A French corps is cut off in the Andalusian heat and surrenders in the open field, the first time a Napoleonic army does so. Napoleon is hundreds of miles away. The news runs through Europe and helps convince Austria to fight again.
fact: Dupont was stripped of his rank and imprisoned when he got home. Napoleon never forgave him.

cmd: Spain: Benito San Juan at Somosierra, Tomás de Morla at Madrid
desc: After pushing the Spanish royal family aside and making his brother Joseph king, he faces a national uprising. He comes in person, wins at Somosierra and retakes Madrid, but the war grinds on for years after he leaves.
fact: This war gave English the word “guerrilla”, Spanish for “little war”. Napoleon later called the conflict his Spanish ulcer.

cmd: France: Napoleon, with Marshal Jean Lannes (mortally wounded)
desc: Crossing the Danube, he is thrown back by Archduke Charles: his first major defeat in person in ten years.
fact: One of his closest friends, Marshal Lannes, was mortally wounded here. It's one of the few times Napoleon was seen weeping on a battlefield.

desc: Six weeks later he crosses the Danube again and wins one of the largest battles Europe had yet seen.
fact: The peace that followed led to his marriage to Marie-Louise of Austria in 1810. She was a great-niece of Marie Antoinette.

cmd: Russia: Michael Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration
desc: The Grande Armée, more than half a million strong, crosses into the Russian Empire. The Russians fall back, burning what they leave behind.
fact: It was one of the most multinational armies ever assembled: Poles, Germans, Italians, Dutch, Swiss and more marched beside the French.

cmd: Britain, Portugal and Spain: Arthur Wellesley, Earl of Wellington
desc: While Napoleon marches into Russia, the other war goes badly. Wellington catches Marmont's army strung out on the march and wrecks half of it in about forty minutes. Madrid falls a few weeks later.
fact: General Foy, who was there, wrote that Wellington had beaten 40,000 men in forty minutes. It changed Wellington's reputation from a cautious defender into a dangerous attacker.

cmd: Russia: Michael Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration
desc: The French take Smolensk, but the Russian army slips away again and leaves the city in flames.
fact: Napoleon thought about stopping here for the winter, then decided to push on to Moscow.

dispute: Counted a French victory because they held the field, but the Russian army was not destroyed and Kutuzov claimed it too.
desc: The Russians finally stand and fight. The French hold the field at the end of the day, but the Russian army survives.
fact: It was the bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars, with roughly 70,000 casualties. Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture commemorates the campaign.

desc: He enters a nearly empty Moscow. Within hours, fires break out across the city.
fact: He waited over a month for the Tsar to negotiate. No answer came, and on 19 October he began the retreat.

cmd: France: Napoleon, with General Jean Baptiste Eblé's bridge builders
Russia: Pavel Chichagov and Peter Wittgenstein
dispute: The crossing itself was a tactical success. It happened inside a strategic disaster, which is why the name became a byword for one.
desc: Trapped by Russian armies at a half-frozen river, what is left of the Grande Armée escapes over two hastily built bridges, at terrible cost.
fact: Engineers stood chest-deep in icy water to build the bridges. In French, “c'est la Bérézina” still means a complete disaster.

cmd: Coalition: Karl Philipp von Schwarzenberg, with General Moreau advising
desc: With a freshly raised army he beats the Allies outside Dresden, his last great victory on German soil.
fact: General Moreau, Napoleon's old French rival, was advising the Allies. He was hit by a French cannonball during the battle and died days later.

cmd: Coalition: Schwarzenberg, Blücher, Bernadotte and Barclay de Tolly
desc: Austria, Prussia, Russia and Sweden combine against him in the Battle of the Nations. He is beaten and driven back across the Rhine.
fact: With around 600,000 soldiers involved, it was the largest battle in Europe until the First World War. Some Saxon units changed sides in the middle of it.

cmd: Coalition: Gebhard von Blücher, with Austrian and Russian corps
desc: Fighting on French soil in sleet, he is beaten by Blücher and falls back. In the weeks after it he wins a run of small, brilliant victories with a tiny army, and it changes nothing: there are always more Allied troops.
fact: The 1814 campaign is often taught as his finest defensive work. It still ended with the Allies in Paris nine weeks later.

desc: With the Allies in Paris and his marshals refusing to fight on, he abdicates.
fact: His farewell to the Old Guard took place in the palace courtyard that is still called the Cour des Adieux, the Courtyard of Farewells.

desc: Sent to the small island of Elba, he keeps the title of Emperor and actually governs it, building roads and reorganising the iron mines.
fact: “Able was I ere I saw Elba” is an English palindrome invented long after. Napoleon himself spoke very little English.

desc: He escapes Elba and lands on the south coast with about a thousand men. Less than three weeks later he is back in Paris.
fact: At Laffrey, troops sent to stop him found him walking toward them, inviting them to shoot their emperor. They joined him instead. His route north is now a scenic road, the Route Napoléon.

cmd: Allies: the Duke of Wellington, with the Prince of Orange
src: Muir, Wellington: Waterloo and the Fortunes of Peace (2015)
desc: On the same afternoon as Ligny, Ney fights Wellington for a crossroads and neither side takes it outright. Wellington pulls back the next day to a ridge at Mont-Saint-Jean, where he will fight Waterloo.
fact: A whole French corps spent the day marching back and forth between the two battlefields and fired a shot at neither.

src: Muir, Wellington: Waterloo and the Fortunes of Peace (2015)
desc: His last victory. He beats Blücher's Prussians but doesn't destroy them.
fact: The 72-year-old Blücher was trapped under his fallen horse and nearly captured, yet was back in the saddle two days later.

cmd: France: Napoleon, with Marshal Michel Ney
Allies: the Duke of Wellington and Gebhard von Blücher
src: Muir, Wellington: Waterloo and the Fortunes of Peace (2015)
desc: Facing Wellington's army, with the Prussians arriving on his flank in the afternoon, he suffers his final defeat. The Hundred Days are over.
fact: Heavy overnight rain delayed his attack while the ground dried, buying the Prussians precious hours. Wellington called it the nearest-run thing he had ever seen.

desc: Exiled by the British to a remote island in the South Atlantic, he dictates his memoirs and dies on 5 May 1821, aged 51.
fact: Rumours of arsenic poisoning still circulate, but most historians accept stomach cancer. In 1840 his remains were brought back to Paris, and he now lies at Les Invalides.
